questions.solution_html:
• Why are powdered spices more susceptible to adulteration than whole spices? [An]/[CO4]
  • Powdered spices are more susceptible to adulteration than whole spices because:
  • • Loss of identity – In powdered form, the original shape, size and structure of the spices are
  • destroyed, making it difficult to visually identify purity.
  • • Easy mixing of adulterants- Cheap substances like starch, husk or colored powders can be easily
  • mixed and go unnoticed in the fine powder
  • Thus, adulteration is harder to detect in powdered spices compared to whole spices

questions.solution_html:
• Write a short note on artificial food preservatives. [U]/[CO1]
  • Artificial or chemical food preservatives are chemical substances added to food to prevent spoilage caused
  • by microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and yeast.They help in extending shelf life, maintaining flavour, colour,
  • and quality of food.These preservatives are added in limited quantities as permitted by food safety laws, and their
  • presence must be declared on food labels.
  • Types of Artificial Preservatives
  • (a) Organic Preservatives-Derived from organic compounds
  • Common examples:Benzoic acid and sodium benzoate – used in fruit juices, soft drinks;Esters of p-hydroxy benzoic
  • acid(Parabens) – used in pickles,softdrinks,syrups,beer and baked foods;Sodium or potassium salts of sorbic acid –
  • used in processed cheese,pickles,bahed foods,bever ages,fish and meat products ;Epoxides- such as ethylene oxide
  • and propylene oxide- used in spices,dried fruits and nuts.
  • (b) Inorganic Preservatives- Simple chemical substances
  • Examples:Sodium and Potassium metabisulphites(Sulphur dioxide (SO₂)) – used in d ried fruits ;Sodium and
  • Potassium Nitrates and nitrites – used in meat preservation
  • Functions include: Inhibit microbial growth,Prevent fermentation and spoilage,Increase storage life,Maintain food
  • quality
  • Advantages are :Increase food availability and storage time,Reduce food wastage,Enable transport of food over long
  • distances,
  • Disadvantages are :Excess use may cause health issues,Some may cause allergic reactions,
  • Strict regulation is required.
  • [Definition+Types with 1 example each+Any 2 functions – 5 marks, Definition+types with examples-4 marks,
  • Definition+types-3 marks, Definition/Types-2 marks, Function/advantages/Disadvantages only-1 mark]

questions.question: Mention one contribution of food chemists in improving nutrition. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the role of oligosaccharides in food flavor and stability. [U]/[CO2]
  • Oligosaccharides are carbohydrates that yield 2 –9 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis. They include
  • disaccharides (e.g., sucrose) and trisaccharides (e.g., raffinose), tetrasaccharides (eg.lychnose). Their role in food
  • systems is important for both flavor and stability.
  • (a) Role in Flavor - Sweetness contribution(Disaccharides like sucrose impart characteristic sweetness an d improve
  • palatability of foods),Flavor enhancement( Oligosaccharides can enhance natural flavors by b alancing acidity and
  • bitterness), Maillard reaction(Some oligosaccharides especially reducing sugars participate in Maillard browning
  • with amino acids, producing desirable flavors, aromas, and c olor in baked and roasted foods),Fermentation
  • substrates(They act as substrates for microorganisms, leading to production of organic acids, alcohols, and flav or
  • compounds in fermented foods).
  • (b) Role in Stability- Moisture retention (Oligosaccharides help in water binding, maintaining softness and preventing
  • drying of food products), Texture improvement (They contribute to viscosity and mouthfeel, improving the consistency
  • of foods like syrups and dairy products), Shelf-life extension (By controlling water activity, they inhibit microbial growth
  • and increase storage stability),Thermal stability (Certain oligosaccharides resist breakdown at moderate temperatures,
  • helping maintain structure during processing).
  • [Definition +any 2 roles each for flavor and stability -5 marks,Roles in flavor only/stability only -3
  • marks,Definition/Classification/Examples only-1 mark]

• Discuss the nutritional functions of proteins in the human body. [U]/[CO2]
  • Proteins perform a variety o functions in the human body and are vital for growth, maintenance, and
  • overall health.Three main functions are structural function,regulatory function and energy fu nction.The different
  • clsses of proteins on the basis of their biological functions are as follows:
  • • Structural Function- Proteins such as keratin and collagen provide mechanical support and structure to tissues
  • like skin, hair, nails, and connective tissues.
  • • Contractile and Movement Function -Proteins like actin and myosin are responsible for musc le contraction and
  • movement, including heartbeat and body motion.
  • • Regulatory Function -Some proteins act as hormones (e.g., insulin and glucagon) and regulate important
  • physiological processes like metabolism and blood glucose levels.
  • • Enzymatic Function -Enzymes are protein in nature and act as biological catalysts, speeding up biochemical
  • reactions in the body (e.g., pepsin and trypsin in digestion).
  • • Storage and Protective Function-Storage proteins (like ferritin) store essential nutrients such as iron, while protective
  • proteins (antibodies or immunoglobulins) help defend the body against infections.
  • • Energy Source (Supplementary)-When required, proteins can be used as a source of energy, providing about 4
  • kcal per gram.
  • • Transportation Function-Some proteins like transferrin is used for the transporting ferric ions in the plasma.
  • [Any 5 functions with explanation-5 marks,Any 4 fns-4 marks,Any3 fns-3 marks and so on.]

questions.question: Discuss the functional properties of minerals in foods. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the Maillard reaction and its impact on protein quality. [A]/[CO2]
  • The Maillard reaction is a non -enzymatic browning reaction that occurs between amino acids ( from
  • proteins) and reducing sugars when food is heated. It is also called the carbonylamine reaction or protein sugar
  • reaction and was named after the French chemist Louis -Camille Maillard. This reaction leads to the formation of
  • brown colour, flavour, and aroma compounds in foods.Rn occurs during heating or prolonged storage of foods.It
  • involves reaction between free amino groups of proteins and carbonyl groups of sugars.It produces desirable flavours
  • in foods like bread crust, roasted coffee, bakery products, and meat.
  • Impact on Protein Quality:
  • • Loss of essential amino acids – especially lysine, as it reacts with sugars and becomes unavailable.
  • • Reduction in protein digestibility due to formation of complex compounds.
  • • Decreased nutritional value of proteins in foods like dried milk powder during storage.
  • • Formation of undesirable browning under low pH and low temperature conditions during long storage.
  • • In some cases, contributes positively by improving taste and aroma, but nutritionally it lowers protein quality.
  • [Correct explanation with impact-5 marks,Explanation of Rn-3 marks,Impact only-3 marks]

questions.question: Discuss the nutritional functions of proteins in the human body. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Write a short note on vitamin K and vitamin C. [U]/[CO3]
  • Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin essential for blood coagulation, bone metabolism, and regulating calcium
  • levels in the body. Known as the "clotting vitamin," or “antihaemorrhagic vitamin” it plays a vital role in enabling
  • blood to clot and stopping wounds from bleeding.
  • Main Forms and Sources :Vitamin K1 (Phylloquinone -Primarily found in green leafy vegetables (s pinach, kale,
  • broccoli, lettuce and vegetable oils. This is the main dietary source. ),Vitamin K2 (Menaquinone - Produced by
  • bacteria in the human gut and found in fermented foods like Natto and some animal products like eggs,
  • cheese),Vitamin K3 (Menadione-A synthetic form that is not used in human nutrition due to potential toxicity.
  • Key Functions: Blood Coagulation (Essential for creating proteins (such as prothrombin) that trigger blood clotting
  • factor production in the liver),Bone Health(Aids in the production of osteocalcin, a protein needed to maintain strong
  • bones and increase bone mineral density),Cardiovascular Health(Helps activate matrix proteins MGP that prevent
  • calcium from depositing in arterial walls, thereby protecting against vascular calcification).
  • Deficiency and Symptoms: Vitamin K deficiency is rare in adults because of its prevalence in the diet and the
  • bacterial synthesis in the gut. However, it can occur in cases of severe malnutrition, fat malabsorption disorders (like
  • Crohn's or Celiac disease), or long -term antibiotic use. Symptoms include increased bruising, nosebleeds, and
  • bleeding that does not stop easily.Newborns: Infants have limited Vitamin K storage, making them prone to Vitamin
  • K Deficiency Bleeding (VKDB), which is why newborns often receive a Vitamin K shot at birth.
  • Vitamin C also known as ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble vitamin essential for human health. Because the body
  • cannot synthesize it, it must be consumed daily through diet.
  • Key Functions: Collagen Synthesis(Crucial for forming collagen, a protein required for healthy skin, cartilage,
  • tendons, ligaments, and blood vessels. ),Antioxidant Protection(Acts as a powe rful antioxidant that protects cells
  • from damage caused by free radicals. ),Immune System Support(Supports immune function and helps white blood
  • cells fight infections ),.Iron Absorption( Enhances t he absorption of non -heme iron,the iron from plant -based
  • foods),Wound Healing(Essential for repairing tissues and forming scar tissue.)
  • Sources:Richest Sources: are kakadu plum, camu camu, acerola, rose hips, and guava.Common Sources are Citrus
  • fruits (oranges, lemons), bell peppers, strawberries, kiwi, broccoli, and tomatoes.
  • Deficiency and Toxicity:A severe lack of vitamin C leads to scurvy, characterized by fatigue,swelling and bleeding
  • of gums, easy bruising, and poor wound healing, loosening of teeth, haemorrhage on the skin and mucous membrane.
  • [Sources,functions and structure of both vitamins-5 marks,functions and sources-3 marks,functions only-2
  • marks,structure only-2 marks,Source and name only-1 mark.]

questions.question: Explain the properties of lipids with reference to their physical, chemical, and nutritional properties. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the properties of lipids with reference to their physical, chemical, and nutritional properties.
  • Lipids form a heterogeneous group of organic compounds which are widely distributed in living systems
  • that have similar solubility properties.They are characterized by their insolubility in water but solubility in organic
  • solvents. eg.oils,fats,waxes etc.Properties of lipids can be classified in physical ,chemical and nutritional properties.
  • a)Physical Properties [U]/[C02]
  • • Solubility – Lipids are hydrophobic and are therefore insoluble in polar solvents like water.However they are soluble
  • in nonpolar or organic solvents such as ether ,chloroform and benzene.
  • • Consistency- The physical state of a lipid (liquid or solid) at roomtemperature depends on its fatty acid
  • composition.Lipids with a high proportion of saturated fatty acids(fats) tend to be solid at room temperature because
  • their straight hydrocarbon chains can pack together tightly.Lipids with more unsaturated fa tty acids (oils) are
  • typically liquid at room temperature because the double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains cause “kinks, " preventing
  • tight packing.
  • • Density : Lipids are less dense than water, causing them to float.
  • • Taste and odour : Pure lipids are generally colourless, odourles,and tasteless. However, they can abso rb flavours
  • and odours from other substances
  • • Energy content : Lipids are energy-rich molecules, providing a high energy yield for life processes.
  • • Charge : Lipid molecules lack an ionic charge, contributing to their hydrophobic (water-repelling) nature.
  • • Amphipathic nature : Some lipids, like phospholipids, are amphipathic, meaning they have both a water -loving
  • (hydrophilic) polar head and a water-fearing (hydrophobic) non-polar tail. This allows them to form cell membranes
  • in an aqueous environment.
  • b)Chemical properties
  • • Hydrolysis: The ester bonds in lipids (triglycerides) can be broken down by reacting with water in a process called
  • hydrolysis. This can be done with either acid or alkali. In acid hydrolysis , triglycerides breaks down into glycerol
  • and fatty acids. In alkaline hydrolysis( saponification) lipid hydrolyse with a strong base (like NaOH or KOH) to
  • form glycerol and fatty acid salts, which are known as soaps.
  • • Hydrogenation: Unsaturated fatty acids, which contain carbon-carbon double bonds, can react with hydrogen
  • gas in the presence of a catalyst (like nickel).This reaction saturates the fatty acid chains by hydrogenating the
  • double bonds, converting a liquid oil into a solid fat. In practice, the hydrogenation is carried ou t by passing
  • hydrogen into the heated oil in the presence of powdered nickel as a catalyst. After hydrogenation, the oil is
  • cooled and the catalyst is removed by filtration.The process is frequently used by the vegetable fat or vanaspati
  • ghee manufacturers.
  • • Halogenation:Halogens such as iodine or bromine can be added across the double bonds of unsaturated fatty
  • acids,decolourising the halogen solution.The iodine number or iodine value measures the degree of unsaturation in
  • a lipid.It is defined as the number of grams of iodine that combines with 100g of oil or fat.
  • c) Nutritional Properties
  • Lipids are essential nutritional components that serve as a concentrated energy source, store energy for later use, and
  • facilitate the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. They also play vital roles in cell membrane structure, hormone
  • production, insulating and protecting organs, and contributing to the taste, texture, and satiety of food.
  • • Energy and Storage- Lipids provide 9 kilocalories per gram, more than double the calories from carbohydrates or
  • proteins, making them an efficient energy source. (High calorific density). The body stores excess energy as fat
  • serving as a long-term energy reserve for times of need(Energy reserve).
  • • Nutrient Absorption and Transport -Lipids are crucial for the absorption of fat soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.(Fat
  • soluble vitamins). By combining with fat-soluble nutrients, lipids increase their bio-availability, meaning the body
  • can absorb them more efficient ly(Bio availability). Lipids also enhance the absorption of beneficial plant
  • compounds.called phytochemicals, such as lycopene and beta carotene.
  • • Cellular and Systemic Functions- Lipids are vital components of all cell membranes, providing structural support
  • and integrity(Cell structure).They form the myelin sheath that insulates nerve cells, protecting them and enabling
  • quick signal transmission throughout the nervous system(Nervous system). Lipids are necessary for the synthesis of
  • vital hormones, including steroid hormones like estrogen and testosterone, which are involved in reproductive health,
  • stress management, and metabolism.(Hormone production).
  • • Protection and Insulation -Lipids help r egulate body temperatuire, providing insulation to help keep the body
  • warm.(Insulation).Adipose tissue provides a physical cushion, protecting vita l organs from injury and
  • damage(Cushioning).
  • • Food Properties-In foods, lipids contribite to desirable aro mas, tastes, and textures, meal(Taste and texture). They
  • also promote feelings of fullness or satiety after a meal(Satiety).
  • [Any 3 physical, chemical and nutritional properties each with explanation -10 marks(minimum of 15
  • points).Any 2 class of properties with explanation-7 marks.Any 1 class of properties-4 marks]

questions.question: What are essential minerals? Explain nutritional roles of essential minerals in human health. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What are essential minerals?Explain nutritional roles of essential minerals in human health? [U]/[CO3]
  • Essential minerals are inorganic elements required by the human body in small amounts for normal growth,
  • metabolism, and maintenance of health. They are inorganic nutrients required for vital body functions, including
  • bone health, fluid balance, muscle contraction, and enzymatic reactions. They are categorized into macrominerals
  • (needed in large amounts) and trace minera ls (needed in small amounts), typically acquired through a balanced
  • diet.They must be obtained through diet because the body cannot synthesize them.
  • • Essential Macrominerals (High Requirement) –Calcium(Builds strong bones and teeth, enables blood
  • clotting, and regulates muscle contraction, including the heart. Sources: Dairy products, leafy greens,
  • tofu.)Magnesium(Maintains muscle/nerve function, immune system, and energy production. Sources:
  • Almonds, spinach, soybeans.)Potassium(Key for fluid balance, nerve signals, and muscle function, reducing
  • blood pressure. Sources: Bananas, potatoes, beans.)Sodium & Chloride(Essential for fluid balance and blood
  • pressure regulation. )Phosphorus(Supports bone mineralization, cell membrane formation, and DNA
  • synthesis.)Sulphur(Crucial for protein structure and metabolism).
  • • Essential Trace Minerals (Small Requirement) - Iron(Essential for producing hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in
  • the blood. Sources: Red meat, lentils, beans. )Zinc(Vital for immune function, wound healing, and DNA synthesis.
  • Sources: Meat, shellfish, nuts ).Iodine(Essential for thyroid hormone sy nthesis, controlling metabolism. )
  • Selenium(Acts as an antioxidant to protect cells and aids thyroid function.), Fluoride (Strengthens teeth and bones,
  • preventing cavities.)Manganese & Chromium(Involved in glucose metabolism and enzymatic processes).
  • Copper(Supports Fe metabolism, connective tissue,andimmunity.)
  • Nutritional Roles of Essential Minerals in Human Health
  • • Structural role (bones and teeth)-Minerals like Calcium and Phosphorus are important for the formation and
  • strength of bones and teeth.
  • • Maintenance of fluid and electrolyte balance-Sodium, Potassium, and Chlorine help regulate osmotic pressure,
  • water balance, and pH of body fluids.
  • • Nerve transmission and muscle contraction -Calcium, potassium, and sodium are essential for proper nerve
  • impulse transmission and muscle contraction, including heart function.
  • • Formation of blood components-Iron is required for hemoglobin formation and oxygen transport. Copper helps
  • in iron metabolism.
  • • Enzyme activation and metabolic functions-Minerals such as Zinc, Magnesium, and Selenium act as cofactors
  • for enzymes involved in metabolism, DNA synthesis, and antioxidant defense.
  • • Hormone production and regulation -Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis, which regulates
  • metabolism and growth.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of food emulsifiers in stabilizing oil water mixtures. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the mechanism of food emulsifiers in stabilizing oil water mixtures. [U]/[CO1]
  • Food emulsifiers are additives used to help mix ingredients that do not naturally combine, such as oil and water.
  • They help to maintain their texture and prevent the ingredients from separating..They blend immiscible ingredients
  • preventing separation, improving texture, and extending shelf life in products like mayonnaise, ice cream, and baked
  • goods. Examples:Lecithin (Used in chocolate, margarine, and baked goods ).Polysorbates (Used in whipped
  • toppings, sauces, and beverages.).DATEM (Diacetyltartaric ester of monoglycerides): Frequently used in bread to
  • strengthen dough. Key Functions- Stabilization,Texture & Mouthfeel,Shelf Life Extension,Aeration etc
  • Mechanism:
  • Emulsifiers are amphiphilic molecules, ie,they have two distinct parts:-Hydrophilic Head: A "water-loving" end
  • that is attracted to water and a hydrophobic Tail: An "oil-loving" end that is attracted to fats and oils.When added to
  • a mixture of oil and water, the emulsifiers migrate to the interface (the boundary where oil and water meet). They
  • position themselves so that their tails point into the oil and their heads point into the water. The emulsifier
  • accumulates at the interface between the two liquid.The presence of emulsifiers at the interface significantly lowers
  • the interfacial tension. This lowers the energy required to break down one phase into tiny droplets (dispersed phase)
  • within the other (continuous phase).The emulsifier forms a thin physical la yer around the dispersed droplets. This
  • protective film around oil droplets, prevent them from grouping back together (coalescing ).Charged heads
  • (especially in ionic emulsifiers) coat the droplets with the same charge, causing them to repel each other.Many
  • stabilizers increase the viscosity of the continuous phase, reducing the movement and collision frequency of
  • droplets.

  • /types only-2 marks]

• (i)Discuss the major components present in ginger
  • (ii) What are the applications of ginger in daily life and medicine? [U]/[CO4]
  • (i) Ginger is the rhizome (a modifie d underground stem) of the Zingiber officinale plant. Its unique
  • characteristics include:
  • • Active Compounds: It contains volatile oils such as zingiberene, ringerone, gingerol, and shogaol.
  • • Flavor: It has a mildly pungent taste with lemony or camphory notes.
  • • Dry Ginger: Known as "chukku," it is more pungent than fresh ginger and is highly valued for adding zest
  • to blander dishes.
  • (ii) Culinary Uses:
  • • Ginger is a versatile ingredient used in various forms:
  • • Whole Root: Used in curries, pickles, chutneys, and preserved dried fruits.
  • Ground Ginger: A common "masala" for dishes like pulao, pongal, and various non-vegetarian preparations.
  • Beverages: Often added to tea, lime juice, and buttermilk for flavor.
  • Murabba: The text notes that ginger is used in making Murabba, a sweet fruit preserve cooked in sugar
  • syrup.
  • Medicinal Benefits
  • Ginger is widely recognized for its therapeutic properties:
  • • Antioxidant: It possesses strong antioxidant properties.
  • • Anti-inflammatory: Reported to reduce inflammation and pain in joints.
  • • Migraine Relief: It has potential prophylactic (preventative) use in treating migraine headaches.
  • • Digestive Aid: Often used to treat stomach-related issues (implied by its volatile oil content).
  • • Alleviating nausea and for motion sickness
  • • Inhibits growth of colon bacteria that cause flatulence
  • • Reduces intestinal contraction,neutralize digestive acids and inhibit the vomiting centre in brain
  • • Detoxification of carcinogens
  • • Natural cough suppressant
